State each assumption before the step that uses it.
A reader processes a derivation line by line,
and a condition that arrives after the line it governs
forces them to go back and reread that line with the condition in mind.
A first-time reader may not realize the line was incomplete,
and may conclude that the step is wrong or unjustified.

This covers every kind of condition:

- a restriction on a variable ("for $x \neq 2$");
- a hypothesis of a theorem;
- a case split;
- a fact that a step relies on.

Introduce the variable and its constraint together,
as in "let $x \neq 2$",
then write the steps that need the constraint.
When a step uses a fact proved earlier,
cite it in the justification on that line.

::: {#exm-assumptions-first}

## Stating the restriction on $x$ before using it

To show that $x = 2$ is a strict local minimizer of $f(x) = (x - 2)^2$,
we show that $f(x) > f(2)$ for every $x$ near 2 other than 2 itself.

> ❌
> $$
> \begin{aligned}
> f(x) - f(2)
> &= (x - 2)^2 - 0 \\
> &> 0
> && \text{(for every } x \neq 2\text{)}
> \end{aligned}
> $$
>
> ✅ Let $x \neq 2$. Then
> $$
> \begin{aligned}
> f(x) - f(2)
> &= (x - 2)^2 - 0
> && \text{(definition of } f\text{)}\\
> &> 0
> && \text{(} x - 2 \neq 0 \text{, so its square is positive)}
> \end{aligned}
> $$

In the ❌ version, the second line is false for $x = 2$,
and the reader learns this only from the note at its end.
In the ✅ version, "let $x \neq 2$" comes first,
so the reader reads each line already knowing which values of $x$ it covers,
and the justification says exactly where the condition is used.

:::
